messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

You have been given a patient's full PTSD profile including their demographics, specific self-reported symptoms, and causal connections between components.
Use ALL of this information to construct a realistic and personalised clinical portrait.

Patient demographics:
  age: 23
  gender: M
  nationality: Israeli
  profession: Student
  pcl5: 43
  trauma_type: Interpersonal

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Seeing the offender,Uncomprehinsible chatter,Being naked
  Negative Appraisals: You can never know who will harm you, I feel isolated and set apart from others, There is something wrong with me as a person
  Memory: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
  Threat: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively?, Having difficulty concentrating?, Trouble falling or staying asleep?
  Maladaptive Strategies: keep mind occupied all the time, ruminate about how to get even with assailant, look down, Seeing other people that were involved in the event or that look similar, Thinking about the event, Going to or near the place where the event happened

Active causal connections (must appear in the vignette):
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat

Forbidden causal connections (must NEVER appear — not explicitly, not implicitly, not narratively):
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Constraints:
- Only include components that appear in at least one active connection.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not in the active list.
- Forbidden links must never be suggested, implied, or hinted at.
- Ground the vignette in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate symptoms.

Output Format:
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Your previous attempt was:
He is a 23-year-old Israeli student who presents with clinically significant post-traumatic distress following an interpersonal trauma. Since the event, his daily life has become organized around a persistent sense of danger and disconnection. He describes feeling set apart from other people, as though something about him has been permanently altered, and he speaks with conviction about a world in which “you can never know who will harm you.” These beliefs now shape much of how he moves through university life and social situations.

Certain cues quickly unsettle him, particularly seeing the offender, hearing incomprehensible chatter, or situations involving being naked. When confronted with these reminders, he becomes sharply on edge and struggles to regain a sense of control. He is more irritable and prone to angry outbursts, finds it hard to concentrate on his studies, and has ongoing difficulty falling or staying asleep. The same moments also intensify his sense that other people are unsafe and unknowable, while reinforcing his belief that there is something wrong with him and that he is fundamentally isolated from others.

Alongside this, his view of himself and others has narrowed. Feeling damaged and separate, he copes by keeping his mind occupied constantly, often looking down and withdrawing from fuller engagement with people around him.

His attempts to manage the aftermath also include repeatedly thinking about the event, ruminating about how to get even with the assailant, and at times seeing other people who were involved or who resemble them, as well as going to or near the place where it happened. These patterns appear to keep him emotionally tied to the trauma and have taken a toll on his relationships, his sense of safety, and his ability to function as a student.

It failed validation. Here is the feedback:
The vignette includes required edges such as Triggers → Threat, Triggers → Negative Appraisals, Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies, and Negative Appraisals → Threat, but it also implies the forbidden edge Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies by describing reminders being followed by attempts to manage the aftermath, including rumination and approaching related people/places. It also suggests Threat → Maladaptive Strategies because his persistent sense of danger/disconnection appears to organize his coping behaviors like constant distraction, looking down, and withdrawal.

Please fix ONLY the flagged violations.
Keep everything else the same.
Do not introduce new causal links that are not in the edge list.

He is a 23-year-old Israeli student who presents with clinically significant post-traumatic distress following an interpersonal trauma. Since the event, his daily life has become organized around a persistent sense of danger and disconnection. He describes feeling set apart from other people, as though something about him has been permanently altered, and he speaks with conviction about a world in which “you can never know who will harm you.” These beliefs now shape much of how he moves through university life and social situations.

Certain cues quickly unsettle him, particularly seeing the offender, hearing incomprehensible chatter, or situations involving being naked. When confronted with these reminders, he becomes sharply on edge and struggles to regain a sense of control. He is more irritable and prone to angry outbursts, finds it hard to concentrate on his studies, and has ongoing difficulty falling or staying asleep. The same moments also intensify his sense that other people are unsafe and unknowable, while reinforcing his belief that there is something wrong with him and that he is fundamentally isolated from others.

His view of himself and others has narrowed. Believing that he is damaged, separate from others, and unable to know who may harm him, he copes by keeping his mind occupied constantly, often looking down and withdrawing from fuller engagement with people around him.

He also spends time repeatedly thinking about the event, ruminating about how to get even with the assailant, and at times seeing other people who were involved or who resemble them, as well as going to or near the place where it happened. These patterns appear to keep him emotionally tied to the trauma and have taken a toll on his relationships, his sense of safety, and his ability to function as a student.
